## The hook

A penguin lives in four measured dimensions — two bill numbers, a
flipper, a mass — and the station wants **one chart** for the annual
report. Any flattening loses information; the craft is choosing *what to
lose*.

A photographer already knows the answer. To capture a whole flock in one
frame, you walk around until you find **the angle that spreads the birds
out most** — shoot down the line of the flock and everyone hides behind
everyone else; shoot across it and the picture holds the most
information a single frame can. **Principal Component Analysis** is that
instinct as linear algebra (M2's dot products, about to earn their keep):
find the direction of maximum spread, then the best remaining
perpendicular direction, and so on — new axes, ranked by how much of the
story each carries.

And this chapter has a twist ending: the module's most quotable honest
lesson, *variance is not relevance*, demonstrated with one unforgiving
number.

> You'll need from before: scaling (Ch9 — PCA is geometry), projections
> via dot products (M2 Ch5), and cluster literacy (Ch17).

---

## See it in two dimensions first

Flipper length and body mass travel together (r = 0.87) — the point
cloud is a cigar. Ask PCA for the photographer's angle:

```{pyodide}
#| caption: "The cigar and its axes: 93.6% of the story lies along one line"
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of scaled flipper length against scaled body mass forming an elongated diagonal cloud. Two arrows radiate from the cloud's centre: a long one labelled PC1 pointing along the cloud's diagonal, and a short perpendicular one labelled PC2. Text notes PC1 carries 93.6 percent of the variance and PC2 6.4 percent."
from lib.data import load_csv
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

feats = ["bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm",
         "flipper_length_mm", "body_mass_g"]
df = load_csv("penguins").dropna(subset=feats)

X2 = StandardScaler().fit_transform(df[["flipper_length_mm",
                                        "body_mass_g"]])
pca2 = PCA().fit(X2)
print("variance carried:", np.round(pca2.explained_variance_ratio_, 3))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.6, 4))
ax.scatter(X2[:, 0], X2[:, 1], s=8, alpha=0.4)
for comp, ratio, name in zip(pca2.components_,
                             pca2.explained_variance_ratio_,
                             ("PC1", "PC2")):
    ax.annotate("", xy=comp * ratio * 3.5, xytext=(0, 0),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", lw=2, color="red"))
    ax.annotate(name, xy=comp * ratio * 3.8, fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlabel("flipper (scaled)")
ax.set_ylabel("mass (scaled)")
ax.set_aspect("equal")
plt.show()
```

PC1 runs along the cigar and carries **93.6%** of the variance; PC2, at
right angles, holds the leftover 6.4%. Nothing was deleted — PCA is a
**rotation**, the same data seen from better axes. Compression happens
only when you *choose* to keep the first few axes and drop the rest.

## Four dimensions, ranked

Now the real table. Scale (mandatory — variance in grams would swamp
variance in millimetres, Chapter 9's hostage crisis in new clothes), fit,
and read the ranking:

```{pyodide}
#| caption: "Four old axes become four ranked ones"
scaler = StandardScaler().fit(df[feats])
Xs = scaler.transform(df[feats])

pca = PCA().fit(Xs)
ratios = pca.explained_variance_ratio_
print("per-axis:   ", np.round(ratios, 3))
print("cumulative: ", np.round(np.cumsum(ratios), 3))
```

PC1 carries 68.8%, PC1+PC2 together **88.2%**. Keep two of four
dimensions, keep seven-eighths of the spread. Do it, and look at the one
chart the station asked for:

```{pyodide}
#| caption: "Four dimensions flattened to two — the clusters survive the squash"
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of the penguins projected onto PC1 and PC2, coloured by species. Three distinct clouds appear: Gentoo well separated on the right, Adelie on the left, and Chinstrap between and below them, overlapping slightly with Adelie. The caption notes this 2-D view preserves 88 percent of the variance."
pca_2 = PCA(n_components=2).fit(Xs)
Z = pca_2.transform(Xs)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.2, 3.6))
for sp in df["species"].unique():
    mask = (df["species"] == sp).to_numpy()
    ax.scatter(Z[mask, 0], Z[mask, 1], s=10, alpha=0.6, label=sp)
ax.set_xlabel("PC1 (68.8% of variance)")
ax.set_ylabel("PC2 (19.3%)")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.show()
```

(Species colours allowed this time — Chapters 17–18 earned the reveal.)
All three clouds survive in two dimensions. This is PCA's everyday job:
faithful maps of high-dimensional data — and relief for Chapter 9's curse
of dimensionality, since distance behaves better in 2 honest dimensions
than in 40 noisy ones.

What did the squash discard? Reconstruct and compare:

```{pyodide}
#| caption: "Decompress a bird and see what two axes couldn't hold"
back = scaler.inverse_transform(pca_2.inverse_transform(Z))

print("bird 0, original:      ",
      [round(v, 1) for v in df[feats].iloc[0]])
print("bird 0, from 2 numbers:", [round(v, 1) for v in back[0]])
```

Bird 0 compressed to two coordinates and decompressed: bills nearly
perfect, flipper 5 mm off, mass off by ~350 g. Two numbers per penguin
instead of four, and this is the cost — measurable, per bird, honest.

## Reading the new axes

What *are* PC1 and PC2? Each is a weighted mix of the old features:

```{pyodide}
#| caption: "The recipe of each principal component"
import pandas as pd

print(pd.DataFrame(np.round(pca_2.components_, 2),
                   index=["PC1", "PC2"], columns=feats))
```

PC1 weights flipper, mass and bill length together (with bill *depth*
opposed) — read it loosely as **overall size**. PC2 is almost pure
**bill shape** (length and depth together, body ignored). Useful
readings — with the standard caution: components are variance
directions, not concepts; naming them is interpretation, and
over-narrating them is a classic way to fool yourself.

## The twist: variance is not relevance

Here is the trap this chapter exists to spring. If PC1+PC2 hold 88% of
the variance, a species classifier on those two components should lose
almost nothing… right? Measure it — one pipeline per component count
(PCA fitted inside the pipeline, on training folds only — Chapter 16's
rule covers *every* fitted transform, this one included):

```{pyodide}
#| caption: "The unforgiving table: PC3 holds 9% of the variance and all of the missing signal"
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

y = df["species"]
for n in (1, 2, 3, 4):
    pipe = Pipeline([("scale", StandardScaler()),
                     ("pca", PCA(n_components=n)),
                     ("model", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))])
    acc = cross_val_score(pipe, df[feats], y, cv=5).mean()
    print(f"{n} component(s): CV accuracy {acc:.3f}")
```

Read it twice. One component: `0.889`. Adding PC2 — 19% of the
variance! — moves accuracy *barely at all* (`0.892`). Adding PC3 — a
mere 9% — leaps to `0.991`, the full-feature score. **PC2 is loud but
says nothing about species; PC3 is quiet and says everything.**

The lesson, worth its own line: **PCA is unsupervised — it ranks
directions by spread, knowing nothing about your target.** Variance
measures how much the data moves along an axis, not whether that
movement matters for your question. So: PCA for maps, compression, and
noise/dimensionality relief — always; PCA as an automatic feature
selector for prediction — only with a measured check like this table,
never on faith.

## Key Takeaways

::: {.key-takeaways}
### Key Takeaways

1. **PCA finds ranked variance directions** — the photographer's angle,
   then the best perpendicular, and so on. It's a rotation; compression
   is the *choice* to keep the first axes. Scale first, always.
2. **Explained-variance ratios** tell how much spread each axis carries:
   68.8 / 19.3 / 9.1 / 2.7% here; two axes kept 88% and all three
   penguin clouds.
3. **Reconstruction shows the cost**: bird 0 from two numbers came back
   with its mass off by ~350 g — compression's bill, itemized.
4. **Components are recipes** over old features (PC1 ≈ overall size,
   PC2 ≈ bill shape) — read loosely; over-narrating them is
   self-deception.
5. **Variance ≠ relevance**: PC2 (19%) added nothing for species; PC3
   (9%) restored 0.892 → 0.991. PCA inside a pipeline, and prediction
   claims measured, never assumed.
:::

### Exercise 2 — Implement (≈8 min) 🟡

Build PCA's atoms from spec, with M2 Ch5's dot product:

- `project(point, direction)` — the point's coordinate along a unit
  direction: the dot product.
- `variance_along(points, direction)` — project every point, then
  return the variance of those coordinates (mean of squared deviations
  from their mean).

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_project
from lib.grader import run_tests
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_project
import math

def project(point, direction):
    """The point's coordinate along a unit direction (dot product)."""
    ...  # TODO

def variance_along(points, direction):
    """Variance of the points' projected coordinates."""
    ...  # TODO

cigar = [(-2.0, -1.0), (0.0, 0.0), (2.0, 1.0)]
along = (2 / math.sqrt(5), 1 / math.sqrt(5))     # the cigar's own axis
across = (-1 / math.sqrt(5), 2 / math.sqrt(5))   # perpendicular to it
run_tests([
    ("projection onto the x-axis", project((3.0, 4.0), (1.0, 0.0)), 3.0),
    ("projection onto a tilted axis",
     round(project((10.0, 0.0), (0.6, 0.8)), 4), 6.0),
    ("spread along the cigar",
     round(variance_along(cigar, along), 4), 3.3333),
    ("no spread across it",
     round(variance_along(cigar, across), 4), 0.0),
], tol=1e-9)
```

<details><summary>If you're stuck</summary>

`project` is `sum(p * d for p, d in zip(point, direction))`. For the
variance: project all points, take the mean of the coordinates, then
average the squared deviations.
</details>

<details><summary>Show solution</summary>

```python
import math

def project(point, direction):
    return sum(p * d for p, d in zip(point, direction))

def variance_along(points, direction):
    coords = [project(p, direction) for p in points]
    mean = sum(coords) / len(coords)
    return sum((c - mean) ** 2 for c in coords) / len(coords)

cigar = [(-2.0, -1.0), (0.0, 0.0), (2.0, 1.0)]
along = (2 / math.sqrt(5), 1 / math.sqrt(5))
across = (-1 / math.sqrt(5), 2 / math.sqrt(5))
```

The last two fixtures are PCA in miniature: along the cigar's own axis
the variance is 3.33, across it exactly 0 — PCA's whole job is finding
the direction that maximizes the quantity you implemented here.
</details>

### Exercise 3 — Stretch (optional, ≈8 min) 🔴

Open-ended, **rubric-graded** (not auto-checked). The chapter sprang the
variance-vs-relevance trap on *species*. Does it spring on **sex** too?
Run the same component sweep (1–4, PCA inside the pipeline) predicting
`df["sex"]` instead (drop rows where it's missing), and report in one
sentence which components carry the sex signal and how that compares
with the species story.

**Rubric — a good answer:**

- Rebuilds the sweep against the sex target with the pipeline pattern
  (no leakage: PCA fitted per fold).
- Reports the accuracy-per-component table.
- The sentence reads it honestly — e.g. if PC1 ("overall size") already
  predicts sex well, that contrasts neatly with species needing quiet
  PC3 — and avoids over-narrating the components while doing so.

<details><summary>Show one possible answer</summary>

```python
d2 = load_csv("penguins").dropna(subset=feats + ["sex"])
for n in (1, 2, 3, 4):
    pipe = Pipeline([("s", StandardScaler()),
                     ("p", PCA(n_components=n)),
                     ("m", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))])
    print(f"n={n}: {cross_val_score(pipe, d2[feats], d2['sex'], cv=5).mean():.3f}")
```

Sex rides mostly on PC1 — bigger birds skew male, so the loud "overall
size" axis does the work that species had to wait for quiet PC3 to get:
which directions matter depends entirely on the question you ask.
</details>

## Where this fits / what's next

The unsupervised trilogy is complete: groups by centres, groups by
merges, and now *directions* — maps that keep the story, ranked axes,
and the module's most transferable warning (variance ≠ relevance,
measure before trusting). One chapter remains, and it is the victory
lap with a deliverable: **the full scikit-learn workflow, end to end,
plus your first model card** — everything since Chapter 1, assembled
into the shape the capstone (and working ML) actually takes.
